summary: For 5–6-year-olds, build the idea that living things don't just live in a habitat — they CHANGE it to meet needs (shelter, food, water, safety). Teach from many vivid, concrete examples (beaver dam → safe pond, bird nest → shelter for eggs, rabbit burrow, tree roots cracking rock and holding soil, squirrel burying nuts, and people building homes or planting gardens), always pairing each change with the need it meets. At this age, 'construct an argument with evidence' means the child states a claim ('this living thing changes its home') and gives a reason ('because it built a dam that made a pond'). Include plants and humans alongside animals so 'organisms' stays broad.
misconceptions: 'Animals only find homes, they don't make/change them' — missing that organisms actively alter their surroundings.
'Only humans change the environment' — not crediting animals and plants.
'Plants don't change anything' — overlooking roots cracking rock and holding soil.
'Animals change things for no reason' — not connecting the change to a need.
'Changing the environment is always harmful' — not seeing it as meeting the organism's needs.

activities.title: Tap the busy habitat: who changed this home, and why?
steps: Explore one rich habitat picture full of organisms that have altered their surroundings.
Tap/point to the beaver and reveal: 'I built this dam to make a deep pond where I'm safe.'
Tap the bird in the tree and reveal: 'I gathered twigs to build a nest so my eggs stay safe.'
Tap the rabbit's burrow and the tree roots splitting a rock, revealing what each organism made and why.
Tap any human-made change in the scene (a house or a planted garden) and reveal that people change their habitat too, to get shelter and food.
For each one, say out loud the change AND the need it meets ('dam → safe pond; nest → shelter for eggs; garden → food').
activities.insight: Each of these living things — animal, plant, and person — has CHANGED its home in a way that helps it get something it needs; many organisms don't just live in a habitat, they reshape it to meet needs.

activities.title: Say the little argument: claim + because
steps: Pick one organism from the habitat (beaver, bird, rabbit, tree roots, or a person).
State the claim out loud: 'This living thing changes its home.'
Give the reason: 'because it ____' (built a dam / gathered twigs / dug a burrow / its roots cracked the rock / built a house).
Add the need: 'so it has ____' (a safe pond / shelter for eggs / a place to hide / room to grow / shelter or food).
Use a 'claim + because' picture sentence frame to support speaking or drawing.
activities.insight: A simple evidence-based argument is a claim plus a 'because' that points to what the organism did and the need it meets.

activities.title: Match the change to the need; sort who changes a home
steps: Match each organism's change to the need it meets: dam ↔ safe pond; nest ↔ shelter for eggs; burrow ↔ safe hiding place; roots ↔ staying anchored and room to grow (the roots crack rock and hold soil); house or garden ↔ shelter or food for people.
Sort examples into 'changes its home' versus organisms that just pass through, to test the distinction.
Answer a picture question such as 'Why did the beaver build a dam?' choosing the need it meets.
activities.insight: Each change exists for a reason — a specific survival need — and many different organisms (animals, plants and humans) change their surroundings.

activities.title: In-role questioning: coax the claim and the because
steps: Talk with a friendly in-role character (a curious ranger, or the beaver itself) who asks: 'What did I change? Why did I do that?'
Answer in your own words, naming the action and the need.
Respond to follow-ups like 'Can a plant change its environment too? How? Can people?' to stretch to new cases.
activities.insight: Children can voice their own reasoning when gently questioned, practising the argument skill the standard names.

activities.title: Build one example: drag sticks to dam the stream
steps: Drag sticks to dam the stream and watch the pond form behind it.
Notice the animal's need being met once the pond appears (safety, water, a home).
Say what you changed and why: 'I dammed the stream, so now there's a deep, safe pond.'
activities.insight: Enacting one case can show that the organism's action CAUSES the change — the pond was not already there.

activities.title: Real-world nature walk complement
steps: On a nature walk, spot real nests, burrows, root-cracked pavement or kerbs, and human-made changes such as houses, paths or gardens.
For each one found, name the organism (animal, plant or person), what it changed, and the need it meets.
Bring back one example to tell as a claim + because.
activities.insight: Organisms changing their habitats is real and all around us — by animals, plants and people — not just in pictures.

checkQuestion: A beaver builds a dam of sticks across a stream and makes a pond behind it. Did the beaver change its environment, or did it just find the pond already there? How do you know — and why would the beaver do it?
checkAnswer: The beaver changed its environment: it built the dam, which blocked the stream and made the pond. We know because the beaver placed the sticks. It does this to meet its needs — the pond gives it safety, water and a place for its home.
